summary: Specifies conventions for using the Camellia encryption algorithm for encryption within the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS). CMS is a general format for protected messages, and this document adds Camellia as an option. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: A lockbox can use different kinds of locks. This says exactly how to use the Camellia lock inside the standard secret-message envelope format.

questions: how does camellia key wrap work
subtitle: Object identifiers and key-wrap rules that let the Camellia cipher protect content in CMS messages.

tldr.problem: The Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) needs unique identifiers and processing rules before a cipher such as Camellia can be used in it for content and key encryption.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3657 defines object identifiers for Camellia in CBC mode (content encryption) and for Camellia key wrap (key encryption), borrows the AES key wrap algorithm, and defines the S/MIME capability encoding.
tldr.outcome: Camellia becomes an optional symmetric algorithm in CMS with 128-, 192- and 256-bit keys. It is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 3657 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 3369, RFC 3370 and RFC 3394.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This document specifies the conventions for using the Camellia encryption algorithm with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS), which is defined in RFC 3369 with algorithms in RFC 3370. It supplies the object identifiers (OIDs) and processing steps so that Camellia can be used for both content encryption and key encryption.

Camellia is added to the set of optional symmetric encryption algorithms in CMS through two classes of OIDs: one class names the content encryption algorithms, the other the key encryption algorithms. A CMS agent applies Camellia by selecting the matching OID and supplying the required parameter.
sections.eli5: The envelope format already exists. This note adds one more lock to the list and gives it a name tag so everyone knows which lock was used.

sections.title: The Camellia Cipher
sections.content:
According to the RFC, Camellia was jointly developed by Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corporation and Mitsubishi Electric Corporation in 2000. It uses a 128-bit block size and 128-, 192- and 256-bit key sizes, the same interface as the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES).

The RFC describes it as suitable for software and hardware, from 32-bit processors to 8-bit smart card processors, with good key setup time and key agility. It states that Camellia was selected as a recommended primitive by the EU NESSIE project and included in the list of techniques for Japanese e-Government systems selected by CRYPTREC.
sections.eli5: Camellia is a scrambling recipe that works on 128-bit chunks and takes a secret key in three sizes, just like AES, so it can slot into the same places.

sections.title: Content Encryption Identifiers
sections.content:
The Camellia content-encryption algorithm in Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) mode has three identifiers, one per key size: id-camellia128-cbc, id-camellia192-cbc and id-camellia256-cbc. They share the same arc prefix and end in camellia128-cbc(2), camellia192-cbc(3) and camellia256-cbc(4).

The AlgorithmIdentifier parameters field MUST be present and MUST contain the initialization vector, defined as CamelliaIV ::= OCTET STRING (SIZE(16)). The plain text is padded according to Section 6.3 of RFC 3369.
sections.eli5: There is one name tag for each key size. The message also carries a random starting value, 16 bytes long, so the same text does not scramble the same way twice.

sections.title: Key Encryption Identifiers
sections.content:
To protect the content-encryption key (CEK), Camellia can wrap it using a Camellia key-encryption key (KEK). Three identifiers cover this: id-camellia128-wrap, id-camellia192-wrap and id-camellia256-wrap. How KEKs are generated and distributed is outside the scope of the document.

For these identifiers, the parameters field MUST be absent, because the key wrap procedure itself defines how and when an IV is used. The OID states the KEK size but says nothing about the size of the wrapped CEK. Implementations MAY use different KEK and CEK sizes, MUST support a KEK and CEK of the same length, and, if different lengths are supported, the KEK MUST be equal to or longer than the CEK.
sections.eli5: The key that scrambles the message is itself locked in a small safe by another key. This part names the safes and says the locking key must be at least as strong as the one inside.

sections.title: The Key Wrap Algorithm
sections.content:
Camellia key wrapping and unwrapping follow the AES key wrap algorithm of RFC 3394, because Camellia and AES have the same block size of 128 bits and key sizes of 128, 192 and 256 bits. Wrapping is identical to Section 2.2.1 of RFC 3394 and unwrapping to Section 2.2.2, with 'AES' replaced by 'Camellia'.

The plaintext is n 64-bit blocks of key data, and wrapping runs s = 6n steps, each encrypting a 64-bit integrity register joined with a data block. The output is n+1 64-bit values. The RFC gives a shifting form and an indexed form that gives identical results and can be computed in place.

The integrity check uses the initial value. The default is the constant A6A6A6A6A6A6A6A6. If unwrapping yields that value, the chance that the key data is corrupt is 2^-64. Any other result MUST make the unwrap return an error and no key data. Alternative initial values are allowed for larger systems, and the RFC notes that, according to RFC 3394, NIST will define them in future publications as needed.
sections.eli5: The key goes into the safe along with a secret check word. When opening the safe, if the check word comes out wrong, you know something was tampered with and you get nothing.

sections.title: S/MIME Capabilities
sections.content:
An S/MIME client SHOULD announce what it supports with the SMIMECapabilities signed attribute (defined in RFC 2633). The list MUST be signed by the client and ordered by preference. A client that must support Camellia symmetric encryption MUST include the Camellia OID in its symmetric category, with the parameter CamelliaSMimeCapability, which is NULL.

The RFC lists the DER-encoded capability for each key size. They differ only in the final arc of the OID: 02, 03 or 04, followed by 05 00 for the NULL parameter.

When a sender picks an algorithm, it considers the recipient's announced capabilities plus private agreements, user preferences and legal restrictions. If users require Camellia, both the sending and receiving S/MIME clients MUST support it and it MUST be set in the user preferences.
sections.eli5: Before sending a secret, you check which locks your friend says they can open. Both of you need to know how to use the Camellia lock, and you both need to pick it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document only specifies Camellia for encrypting CMS message content and for encrypting the key that protects that content. The other mechanisms are the same as existing ones, so the security considerations of the CMS specifications (RFC 3369 and RFC 3370) and of the AES key wrap algorithm (RFC 3394) apply. The RFC also states that no security problem has been found on Camellia, citing CRYPTREC and NESSIE.

The Intellectual Property Statement adds that the IETF was notified of intellectual property rights claimed in regard to some or all of the specification.
sections.eli5: Nothing new is invented here, so the safety advice for the old envelope and AES key safe still applies. The authors say no weakness had been found in Camellia.
